clinicalPearls: Presents as a rapidly growing, dome-shaped, flesh-coloured nodule with a central keratin-filled crater, typically on sun-exposed skin of older, fair-skinned patients.
Classically follows a triphasic natural history of rapid proliferation, a stationary phase and then spontaneous involution over months, often leaving a depressed scar.
Widely regarded as a well-differentiated variant of squamous cell carcinoma that cannot be reliably distinguished from invasive disease on clinical or histological grounds.
Complete excision with a deep margin is generally preferred, because superficial or partial biopsy may miss an invasive squamous cell carcinoma at the base.
Multiple lesions suggest a syndrome: Ferguson-Smith type (multiple self-healing), Grzybowski type (eruptive) or Muir-Torre syndrome with sebaceous neoplasms and visceral malignancy.
Associations include ultraviolet exposure, immunosuppression, trauma and BRAF inhibitor therapy.
Dermoscopy typically shows a central keratin mass with surrounding white structures and looped vessels.
Histology shows a central keratin plug with buttressing (lipping) epidermal edges and a glassy, well-differentiated keratinocyte proliferation.
reference.pathophysiology: Keratoacanthoma arises from a neoplastic proliferation of keratinocytes, thought to originate from the follicular infundibulum, driven largely by ultraviolet-induced DNA damage and, in some cases, immunosuppression, trauma or drug exposure such as BRAF inhibitors. The proliferative phase produces the characteristic crateriform nodule, while a cell-mediated immune response is believed to underlie the spontaneous involution seen in many lesions. Because the proliferation shares molecular and morphological features with well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, the two exist on a continuum.
additionalDifferentials: Merkel cell carcinoma or deep fungal infection
additionalInvestigations: Excisional biopsy that includes the deep base to allow assessment for invasion
Dermoscopy showing central keratin and peripheral white circles or looped vessels
Review of immunosuppression status and drug history including BRAF inhibitors
Assessment for multiplicity and family history to identify a syndromic cause
Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry and colonoscopy when Muir-Torre syndrome is suspected
Regional lymph node examination if invasive squamous cell carcinoma is confirmed
redFlags: Ulceration, induration or continued rapid growth without the expected involution
Lesions on the lip, ear or in a periungual or mucosal site, where malignant behaviour is more likely
Recurrence after treatment or perineural symptoms
Multiple or eruptive lesions suggesting an underlying syndrome or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Although many lesions involute spontaneously, they leave scars and cannot be reliably distinguished from invasive squamous cell carcinoma, so complete excision is recommended and generally curative, with an excellent outcome.
pitfalls: Assuming a lesion is benign and observing it, thereby missing an invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
Relying on a superficial shave or partial biopsy that fails to sample the tumour base.
Overlooking Muir-Torre syndrome in patients with multiple or atypical lesions.
Failing to consider drug-induced lesions in patients on BRAF inhibitor therapy.
